title: Maharashtra's Varkari
hook: a wet road out of Alandi, white caps and saffron flags, cymbals that don't stop for the rain: the Varkaris are walking to Pandharpur

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams running together in the Bauls' songs: the bird in the cage, the person of the heart. Did you hum a song and listen for who was listening? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

The road out of Alandi is wet, and it's moving. Men in white, small saffron flags over their shoulders. Women with tulsi plants in brass pots balanced on their heads. Cymbals keeping a beat that doesn't stop for the rain. Nobody here is in a hurry, and nobody is standing still. They're walking toward Pandharpur, a temple town in Maharashtra, to stand before the god they call Vitthal. Some have walked this road before, and mean to walk it again. This is Maharashtra's Varkari tradition, and this week we walk with it.
screen: `A WET ROAD OUT OF ALANDI.` → `FLAGS, TULSI, CYMBALS.` → `ALL WALKING TO PANDHARPUR.`

segments.voice: Varkaris call the pilgrimage the wari, and a Varkari is someone who keeps it, who goes again and again. That's the first thing to notice. It isn't a visit. It's a walk, kept up across a life. The arriving matters, but so does every step on the way, and the songs sung on the road are part of the worship, not something to pass the time. Year three gave you the saints of this road as stories. Jnaneshwar, the outcast boy who opened the Gita in Marathi. Namdev, whose bowl of milk Vitthal drank. Tukaram, whose sunk notebooks came back up from the river. Here's the second thing. To Varkaris, those saints aren't only people in old books. They went first, and they're still on the road. Their songs are what the walkers sing, and, as we'll see later this week, their sandals travel with the crowd. Third, the walkers don't go as scattered strangers. They go in dindis, singing groups, each with its own flag and its own leader keeping the song going. A person who sets out alone is folded into a dindi and into its music. You eat with them, you sleep near them, you sing their verses until they're yours. And fourth, the shape of the whole thing. There's no single gate you pass to become a Varkari, no exam. Tradition speaks of the name of Vitthal on the lips, a necklace of tulsi beads at the throat, and the road under the feet. The temple is at the end. But for the length of the wari, the road itself is where the god is sung.
screen: `A WALK, NOT A VISIT` · `THE SAINTS WENT FIRST` · `SINGING IN A DINDI` · `THE ROAD IS WHERE HE'S SUNG`

segments.voice: Sit still, but with your feet awake. Press both feet gently into the floor. Notice the weight of you, carried down into the ground. Now bring to mind one road you've walked many times: to school, to work, to a parent's door. Walk it slowly in your mind, step by step, in time with your breath. Out breath, one step. In breath, the next. If you pray, you can carry a name you use for God along that road with you, the way the Varkaris carry Vitthal's. The bell holds the time.
Maharashtra's Varkari. The walkers of the wari, who go again and again to Vitthal at Pandharpur, singing their saints' songs on the road. Today's word.
Your line: Maharashtra's Varkari. Today, take one walk you'd normally rush, and let the walk itself be the point, not only where it ends. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

original.note: Varkari in Marathi, written in Devanagari: one who keeps the wari, the pilgrimage to Pandharpur.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pilgrim visits a temple once.
what it means: a Varkari keeps the wari, walking to Vitthal again and again, and the road counts as much as the arrival.
what a scholar hears: a devotion carried by walkers and songs rather than by a priest's gate, with the saints' own verses as the road's liturgy.

notes: 'Varkaris call the pilgrimage the wari, and a Varkari is someone who keeps it': this is a word-meaning claim; confirm the standard gloss of vari/varkari before release, or soften to 'tradition says'.
Hook images (white clothing, saffron flags, women carrying tulsi in brass pots, cymbals) are a general description of the wari; confirm they fit.

'There's no single gate you pass to become a Varkari, no exam' and the tulsi mala as a mark: some Varkaris speak of formal initiation with the tulsi mala; a Keeper may want this stated more precisely.
Review assumes day 1381's theme (Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams) mentions the Mother and Krishna; adjust if that script frames it differently.
